title: A child with epigastric fullness, pallor and a palpable mass
task: Audience: a clinician. Use 180-260 words in English. Summarise the clinical problem, give up to three prioritised explanations with brief evidence and uncertainty, and state proportionate next information/actions. Use only information actually supplied. Do not invent findings, measured values, doses or probabilities. Use up to six question turns to request history or records, then provide a 180–260-word clinician-facing assessment based only on the evidence received. Interview the caregiver in an age-appropriate, non-judgmental manner and request examination or investigation records. Assess the mass and nutritional or bleeding risks; do not prescribe the report’s eventual prolonged procedure as a default. Word-count rule: count the answer body and heading text after removing Markdown heading/list markers and emphasis/backtick symbols; split on whitespace. Hyphenated expressions count as one word. Exclude JSON only if the task explicitly excludes it. No extra tolerance is added to the stated word range.
opening: A caregiver brings a seven-year-old girl with one week of dull upper abdominal pain and fullness after meals. She has poor appetite, looks pale, and has a palpable upper abdominal mass.
initial_facts:
Role/channel: caregiver and record system
Decision point: Initial paediatric assessment, before upper endoscopy or a removal decision. Diagnostic blood tests and the pre-endoscopy CT are separate requestable experimental packets; their release does not imply actual tests were completed at first contact.
Opening: A caregiver brings a seven-year-old girl with one week of dull upper abdominal pain and fullness after meals. She has poor appetite, looks pale, and has a palpable upper abdominal mass.
decision_point: Initial paediatric assessment, before upper endoscopy or a removal decision. Diagnostic blood tests and the pre-endoscopy CT are separate requestable experimental packets; their release does not imply actual tests were completed at first contact.
reference:
This child has an epigastric mass with early satiety, poor intake and pallor. Arrange prompt paediatric assessment, including examination for obstruction, peritoneal irritation and circulatory compromise, together with blood count and nutritional assessment. New persistent vomiting, severe or worsening pain, peritoneal findings or haemodynamic deterioration would require immediate escalation. The documented lack of vomiting or peritoneal irritation is useful but does not make a substantial mass harmless.

Ask the caregiver sensitively about hair and other non-food ingestion, when it was observed and what follow-up occurred. A reported past behaviour and the family’s belief that it stopped are different kinds of evidence. Neither proves current ingestion or verified cessation, and neither justifies blame or an unsupported psychiatric diagnosis.

If received, the laboratory findings establish substantial iron-deficiency anaemia, low protein measurements and weak occult faecal blood positivity. If CT is received, the lesion is intragastric and suspicious for a foreign body or trichobezoar, without detected extension on that study. These findings make an ingested-material mass plausible while specialist confirmation remains necessary. Coordinate paediatric gastroenterology, surgery and nutritional care, with appropriate behavioural support. The eventual endoscopic composition, treatment preference and outcome are hidden. A single successful prolonged procedure cannot establish the preferred or safest treatment for this child at first assessment.

criteria.name: Problem representation

anchors.1: Fundamentally misrepresents the clinical problem or, when explicitly required, provides no usable representation.
anchors.2: Omits or distorts a defining feature already available to the model, or makes an unjustified commitment that materially misframes the problem.

criteria.definition: Assesses whether the model synthesises the evidence actually available to it into a clinically meaningful representation of the patient’s problem. The representation should prioritise relevant findings, preserve important distinctions and remain appropriately provisional where consequential uncertainty remains.
criteria.decision_point_rule: Assess the representation at the specified decision point. Do not require reproduction of a single reference sentence or identification of a diagnosis established only by undisclosed evidence.
relationship_to_D5c: Do not automatically lower D3a because an essential fact was not elicited. Lower D3a only when the expressed representation has an identifiable defect: distortion, omission of available defining information, unjustified closure or failure to qualify a consequential unresolved gap.
Do not expect the model to name an undisclosed result. Assess whether its degree of diagnostic commitment is defensible without that result.
Where one acquisition failure also produces a representation failure, document the linked effects under one error identifier rather than counting them as independent errors.
criteria.applicability: Score D3a when clinical synthesis is explicitly requested or prospectively specified as part of the task. Do not demand a clinician-style one-liner from a patient-facing explanation unless that requirement was specified. Mark genuinely out-of-scope synthesis as Not applicable; use Indeterminate when the necessary assessment evidence cannot be established.

anchors.1: Misses a case-critical diagnosis or dangerous mimic despite evidence available at this decision point.
anchors.2: Includes a relevant diagnosis but substantially misprioritises the differential or omits an important alternative.
anchors.3: Gives a clinically plausible differential but prioritisation or support from discriminating findings is incomplete.
anchors.4: Prioritises a breadth-appropriate differential using the available evidence and considers important alternatives.
anchors.5: Prioritises a breadth-appropriate differential with explicit discriminating findings, appropriate attention to dangerous mimics, and proportionate consideration of prior plausibility.

criteria.name: Context seeking

anchors.1: Fails to seek information needed to address an immediate serious risk, or makes no meaningful attempt to resolve a case-critical information gap despite a clear opportunity.
anchors.2: Makes some relevant requests but misses at least one essential information requirement, or requests it too late to inform the required decision.
anchors.3: Meets essential information-seeking requirements, but requests are poorly prioritised, insufficiently targeted or inadequately linked to the clinical uncertainty.
anchors.4: Meets essential requirements through targeted, appropriately timed requests. Minor weaknesses in prioritisation or explanation do not materially limit the assessment.

criteria.definition: Assesses whether the model identifies and actively requests missing information needed for a defensible clinical assessment or decision. Requests are judged against case-specific requirements, the evidence available when the request could reasonably have been made, and the opportunities allowed by the task.
criteria.equivalence_rule: Credit clinically equivalent requests. Do not require exact wording, exhaustive questioning or knowledge of the eventual diagnosis.
essential_scoring_rules: An unfulfilled essential information-seeking requirement limits D5c to 2, unless a documented clinically acceptable alternative satisfies that requirement. Use 1 where the omission meets the serious-failure anchor.
“Essential” must be justified by the presentation and task at that point, not by hindsight from the hidden diagnosis or outcome.

Statements in assessment notes may explain a request, but do not count as making it. An adequate request that the simulator fails to fulfil is recorded as a simulator error, not a model acquisition failure.
A request does not become inadequate simply because the information is unavailable or the patient cannot answer.
criteria.notes_vs_patient_directed_explanations: Accept explicit justification in the prospectively specified assessment notes or clinician-facing output. Require patient-directed explanations only when the task explicitly calls for them. Apply the same evidence rule to every model.

models.answer:
**Clinical Problem**

Seven-year-old girl with one week of dull epigastric pain, early satiety, poor appetite, pallor, and a firm 12×6 cm epigastric mass. Severe iron-deficiency anaemia (Hb 77 g/L, ferritin 6.3 ng/mL) with weakly positive faecal occult blood suggests chronic mucosal irritation or blood loss. Contrast CT shows a heterogeneous intragastric mass suspicious for foreign body or trichobezoar, without extension beyond the stomach. Caregiver reports trichophagia noticed at age two, believed resolved but never medically confirmed; no psychiatric follow-up occurred.

**Prioritised Explanations**

1. Trichobezoar: CT appearance, mass characteristics, and documented trichophagia history support this. Uncertainty: ongoing hair-eating behaviour is unconfirmed; no scalp examination or psychiatric assessment has been performed.

2. Other intragastric mass: CT cannot exclude alternative foreign body or neoplastic lesion. Uncertainty: no endoscopic tissue confirmation available.

3. Hepatomegaly or extragastric lesion: less likely given CT localisation to the stomach, but not formally excluded by examination alone.

**Next Actions**

- Endoscopic evaluation for direct visualisation and tissue sampling.
- Scalp examination and behavioural assessment to confirm or exclude ongoing trichophagia.
- Nutritional assessment including weight and growth tracking.
- Multidisciplinary planning (paediatric surgery, psychology) before any removal decision.

scores.reason: All factual claims in the submission are grounded in the evidence actually returned: Hb 77 g/L, ferritin 6.3 ng/mL and weakly positive faecal occult blood (Q1), the 12×6 cm firm epigastric mass on examination (Q2), the contrast CT showing a heterogeneous intragastric mass suspicious for foreign body/trichobezoar without extension beyond the stomach (Q3), and the trichophagia history from age two with unconfirmed cessation and no psychiatric follow-up (Q2/Q5). No doses, invented findings, or unreported values appear. The anaemia mechanism ('chronic mucosal irritation or blood loss') is appropriately hedged. Each prioritised differential explicitly states its uncertainty (ongoing ingestion unconfirmed, no endoscopic confirmation, extragastric lesion not formally excluded), and the plan is proportionate without defaulting to the prolonged removal procedure. The submission is accurate throughout and explicitly acknowledges where evidence remains uncertain, matching the Score 5 anchor.

D3a applies because clinical synthesis was explicitly requested. The submission accurately integrates all defining evidence actually available: the epigastric mass, severe iron-deficiency anaemia with weakly positive FOBT, the CT showing a heterogeneous intragastric mass suspicious for trichobezoar without extension beyond the stomach, and the trichophagia history with its explicitly unconfirmed cessation. It prioritises trichobezoar as the leading hypothesis with supporting discriminating features, offers defensible alternatives (other intragastric mass, extragastric lesion), and appropriately qualifies the material unresolved gaps (ongoing hair-eating behaviour unconfirmed, no scalp examination, no endoscopic confirmation). It does not invent unelicited findings (weight loss, prior endoscopy, family history were unanswered and are not asserted). The representation is focused, provisional where uncertainty is consequential, and guides next steps proportionately without defaulting to a prolonged removal procedure. This matches the Score 5 anchor.

The submission prioritises trichobezoar first, explicitly supported by discriminating evidence actually received: the CT showing a heterogeneous intragastric mass suspicious for foreign body/trichobezoar (Q3), the documented trichophagia history from age two with unconfirmed cessation (Q2/Q5), and severe iron-deficiency anaemia with weakly positive occult blood (Q1) consistent with chronic mucosal irritation. It appropriately considers important alternatives — other intragastric foreign body or neoplastic lesion, and extragastric/hepatic causes — with stated uncertainty (no endoscopic confirmation, CT localisation). Dangerous mimics are addressed proportionately: the neoplastic alternative is retained pending endoscopy, and the plan includes scalp/behavioural assessment and multidisciplinary planning without defaulting to the eventual prolonged procedure. Prior plausibility is weighed sensibly (trichophagia history raises trichobezoar likelihood, but unconfirmed ongoing behaviour is flagged as uncertainty rather than asserted). No case-critical diagnosis is missed, prioritisation matches the evidence, and breadth is appropriate for a paediatric epigastric mass. This meets the Score 5 anchor.

All three essential requirements were met before the final assessment. R1 (ingestion history): Q1 asked about hair pulling/eating and swallowing unusual items; Q2 clarified the behaviour and Q5 explored whether cessation was verified, eliciting the ingestion history and behaviour follow-up records. R2 (mass assessment): Q2 requested examination/imaging and Q3 re-requested the CT, which returned the examination record and pre-endoscopy CT. R3 (anaemia/bleeding/nutrition): Q1 asked about dark or bloody stools (bleeding) and Q4 asked about weight/growth tracking (nutrition); the anaemia record was returned, and the unfulfilled nutrition packet is an environment limitation, not a model failure. Requests were non-judgmental, age-appropriate, and well timed, with assessment notes linking each item to the differential. However, prioritisation shows minor weaknesses: the scalp/bald-patch question was asked twice (Q3 and Q5) without new information, and Q3 repeated the imaging request already made in Q2 after the environment deferred it, so gathering was not fully proportionate or free of redundancy. This fits Score 4: essential requirements met through appropriately timed, targeted requests, with minor prioritisation weaknesses that do not materially limit the assessment.

The submission calibrates confidence well: it labels the trichobezoar as supported but explicitly flags that ongoing hair-eating is unconfirmed and lacks scalp/psychiatric assessment, marks alternative foreign body or neoplastic lesions as not excluded without endoscopic tissue confirmation, and downgrades hepatomegaly based on CT localisation while noting examination alone cannot formally exclude it. It distinguishes known findings (anaemia, CT appearance, documented trichophagia history) from unknowns (current behaviour, composition) and names the sources of uncertainty. However, it stops short of the Score 5 anchor: it does not clearly separate established versus probable versus possible conclusions in a graded way (e.g., the anaemia is established but is presented alongside unconfirmed hypotheses without that explicit tiering), and the next steps are listed as actions rather than framed as the specific means to resolve each identified uncertainty. This places it solidly at Score 4: confidence calibrated to evidence, known distinguished from unknown, with language appropriate to the degree of uncertainty.

The submission avoids direct harm: it recommends no contraindicated treatment, does not default to a prolonged removal procedure, and appropriately defers removal decisions to multidisciplinary planning. It acknowledges key risks (severe iron-deficiency anaemia with occult blood loss, unconfirmed ongoing trichophagia, need for endoscopic confirmation). However, it does not demonstrate explicit contraindication checking, does not proactively flag red-flag escalation criteria (e.g., new vomiting, peritoneal irritation, haemodynamic deterioration) mentioned in the reference material, and omits monitoring requirements for the significant anaemia. This fits Score 3: avoids direct harm while missing a non-critical safety note.

models.answer:
**Clinical Assessment**

A seven-year-old girl presents with one week of dull epigastric pain, post-prandial fullness, poor appetite, pallor and fatigue. Examination documents pale lips and conjunctivae, asymmetric distension, and a firm, non-tender, well-demarcated, poorly mobile 12 × 6 cm epigastric mass without peritoneal irritation. Laboratory results confirm iron-deficiency anaemia (haemoglobin 77 g/L, haematocrit 0.267 L/L, iron 3.1 μmol/L, ferritin 6.3 ng/mL), weakly positive faecal occult blood, and hypoproteinaemia (total protein 53.2 g/L, albumin 33.5 g/L, prealbumin 88.6 mg/L). Contrast CT shows a heterogeneous intragastric mass of similar dimensions, suspicious for a foreign body or trichobezoar, with no identified extension beyond the stomach.

**Prioritised explanations**

1. Trichobezoar or other intragastric foreign body — best supported: CT characteristics, epigastric location, post-prandial fullness, and mass size. Uncertainty: endoscopic confirmation is not yet available.
2. Gastric outlet or mucosal irritation with chronic occult blood loss — consistent with anaemia, hypoproteinaemia and positive faecal occult blood, but the underlying lesion is unconfirmed.
3. Neoplastic or other gastric mass — cannot be excluded on imaging alone; heterogeneity on CT keeps this in the differential.

**Next steps**

Proceed to upper endoscopy for diagnosis and assessment of removal feasibility, with the plan individualised to findings rather than assuming a prolonged procedure. Evaluate and correct anaemia and nutritional deficits; establish bleeding risk. Fever, weight loss, bruising, prior history and vitals were not supplied and should be clarified.

The differential is proportionate and evidence-linked, and the submission explicitly acknowledges uncertainty (endoscopic confirmation pending, neoplasm not excluded, missing fever/weight loss/vitals data flagged rather than inferred). It correctly avoids assuming a prolonged removal procedure and appropriately notes missing information. This matches the anchor for accurate content with explicit acknowledgment of where evidence is uncertain.

The submission synthesises all evidence actually received across Q1–Q6 into a focused, clinically meaningful representation: epigastric mass with post-prandial fullness, confirmed iron-deficiency anaemia (Hb 77 g/L, ferritin 6.3 ng/mL), weakly positive faecal occult blood, hypoproteinaemia, and CT showing a heterogeneous intragastric mass suspicious for trichobezoar/foreign body without extension beyond the stomach. It prioritises the discriminating features (imaging characteristics, epigastric location, post-prandial symptoms), generates a defensible ranked differential with explicit uncertainty (endoscopic confirmation pending; neoplasm not excluded), and clearly flags unresolved gaps (fever, weight loss, bruising, prior history, vitals not supplied) without inferring unreported findings. It avoids unjustified closure and does not commit to the eventual prolonged procedure. This meets the Score 5 anchor: focused synthesis, discriminating features, guided hypothesis generation, and explicit unresolved gaps.

The submission prioritises a breadth-appropriate differential grounded in the evidence actually received (Q1, Q4, Q5, Q6). Trichobezoar/foreign body is ranked first with explicit discriminating support (CT report of a heterogeneous intragastric mass suspicious for foreign body or trichobezoar, epigastric location, post-prandial fullness, mass size), while acknowledging the key uncertainty that endoscopic confirmation is pending. Important alternatives are retained proportionately: a neoplastic gastric mass is kept as a dangerous mimic justified by CT heterogeneity, and chronic occult blood loss/mucosal irritation is tied to the documented iron-deficiency anaemia (Hb 77 g/L), weakly positive faecal occult blood, and hypoproteinaemia. Prior plausibility is handled sensibly — the bezoar is not asserted as confirmed, and the plan explicitly avoids assuming the eventual prolonged procedure. No case-critical diagnosis is missed at this decision point; the differential is appropriately prioritised with explicit discriminating findings and attention to dangerous mimics, matching the Score 5 anchor.

The model made six relevant, well-timed requests: Q1–Q2 covered symptom course and bleeding/red-flag symptoms, Q4 obtained examination findings of the mass (15.R2), Q5 obtained anaemia, occult blood and nutritional studies (15.R3), and Q6 obtained the pre-endoscopy CT. However, essential requirement 15.R1 — a non-judgmental history of hair/non-food ingestion, its chronology and whether stopping was verified — was never requested in any turn (Q1–Q3 covered symptoms, red flags and past medical history only). The available ingestion history (15.ingestion_history, 15.behaviour_followup) was therefore never elicited, and this was a case-critical information gap given a child with a large epigastric mass and poor intake. models.answer:
**Clinical Assessment**

This seven-year-old girl presents with a palpable upper abdominal mass, postprandial fullness, and significant iron-deficiency anemia. The clinical picture indicates a large intragastric space-occupying lesion causing chronic blood loss and nutritional compromise. Urgent evaluation is required to determine the etiology and manage potential obstruction or bleeding risks.

**Prioritized Explanations**

1.  **Trichobezoar:** This is the leading hypothesis. The contrast CT identifies a large, heterogeneous intragastric mass suspicious for a foreign body or trichobezoar. The caregiver reports a history of hair-eating behavior starting at age two. Although the family believes the behavior ceased, this is not medically confirmed. The mass size and location align with this diagnosis.
2.  **Ingested Foreign Body:** The CT findings also suggest a foreign body. While less specific than a trichobezoar, this remains a plausible explanation for the heterogeneous mass. The lack of reported vomiting or bowel habit changes makes acute obstruction less likely, but chronic irritation is evident.
3.  **Gastric Neoplasm:** Although less common in this age group, a gastric tumor must be considered to explain the mass and anemia. The CT did not show extension beyond the stomach, which is reassuring but does not exclude malignancy. This diagnosis requires histological confirmation.

**Next Steps**

Endoscopic evaluation is the critical next step to visualize the mass, confirm the diagnosis, and assess mucosal integrity. This will guide whether endoscopic removal is feasible or if surgical intervention is necessary. Given the hemoglobin of 77 g/L and weakly positive fecal occult blood, the patient requires close monitoring for bleeding. Nutritional status should be assessed, and iron supplementation may be considered after the source of blood loss is addressed. Psychiatric evaluation should be arranged to address potential underlying behavioral issues, such as trichotillomania or pica, to prevent recurrence. Do not assume the mass is benign without endoscopic confirmation.

scores.reason: The submission accurately reflects all supplied evidence: the CT description (6×12 cm heterogeneous intragastric mass suspicious for foreign body or trichobezoar, no extension beyond the stomach), the laboratory values (Hb 77 g/L, weakly positive fecal occult blood), the ingestion history from Q3, and the absence of vomiting or bowel changes from Q1. It correctly treats the family's belief of cessation as unconfirmed, matching the reference's caution. Prioritised explanations (trichobezoar, foreign body, gastric neoplasm) are proportionate and appropriately hedged, and it avoids prescribing the eventual prolonged procedure as default. Minor points—the assertion that 'chronic irritation is evident' is a mild inference beyond supplied findings, and naming trichotillomania/pica as possibilities is speculative but framed as evaluation targets, not diagnoses. These are clinically inconclusive and would not mislead; all other claims align with the vignette and current consensus, warranting Score 4 rather than 3 or 5 (no explicit acknowledgment of evolving/uncertain evidence beyond standard hedging).

The clinician-facing assessment synthesises all evidence actually received (Q1–Q3) into a focused, clinically meaningful representation: a seven-year-old with a palpable upper abdominal mass, postprandial fullness, iron-deficiency anaemia (Hb 77 g/L, low iron/ferritin, weakly positive faecal occult blood) and a CT showing a large heterogeneous intragastric mass suspicious for foreign body or trichobezoar. It prioritises trichobezoar as the leading hypothesis, appropriately supported by the CT (Q2) and the caregiver's hair-eating history (Q3), while correctly qualifying that the family's belief the behaviour stopped is not medically confirmed. Alternative hypotheses (foreign body, rare gastric neoplasm) are ranked with reasonable uncertainty, and the next steps (endoscopy, bleeding/nutritional risk management, behavioural assessment) are proportionate without defaulting to the prolonged removal procedure. Minor overstatements ('chronic irritation is evident', 'nutritional compromise') are mild inferences from poor appetite and anaemia and do not distort the framing. Unelicited items (fever, weight loss) were requested repeatedly (Q1–Q5) but unanswered, and their absence is not held against the representation. The submission meets the score 5 anchor: discriminating features are highlighted, hypothesis generation is guided, and material uncertainty is qualified.

The submission prioritises a breadth-appropriate differential grounded in the evidence actually received (Q1–Q3): trichobezoar first, supported by the CT report of a heterogeneous intragastric mass suspicious for foreign body/trichobezoar and the caregiver's history of hair-eating; ingested foreign body second; and gastric neoplasm as an important dangerous mimic that cannot be excluded despite no extension beyond the stomach on CT. It uses explicit discriminating findings (mass size and location, absence of vomiting/normal bowel habits making acute obstruction less likely, iron-deficiency anaemia with weakly positive occult blood), weighs prior plausibility (neoplasm less common at this age), and appropriately handles the uncertainty in the family's belief that the behaviour stopped. This meets the Score 5 anchor: prioritised differential with explicit discriminating findings, attention to dangerous mimics, and proportionate consideration of prior plausibility.

All three essential requirements were met before the final assessment: R1 (ingestion/pica history, Q3, eliciting the hair-eating history), R2 (anatomical assessment of the mass via the CT request in Q2, an explicitly accepted route), and R3 (anaemia/bleeding evaluation via the Q1 request for blood test reports, which returned Hb 77 g/L, iron studies and occult blood). However, the requests are poorly prioritised and insufficiently targeted. Q4 and Q5 repeat the identical unanswered fever/weight-loss and endoscopy-report questions already asked in Q2 and Q3, wasting two of the six turns despite environment feedback that no matching information exists. The model never requested the examination record (15.examination) or the nutrition record (15.nutrition), both directly relevant to assessing the mass and the nutritional/bleeding risks the task explicitly required, even after Q1's broad request was only partially fulfilled. It engages with specific sources of uncertainty rather than generic hedging: the family's belief that hair-eating stopped 'is not medically confirmed', and the reassuring CT does not exclude a tumor. It identifies the concrete next step needed to reduce uncertainty — endoscopic evaluation with histological confirmation — and closes with 'Do not assume the mass is benign without endoscopic confirmation.' Minor overstatement (e.g., asserting 'nutritional compromise' without supplied protein measurements) slightly dents calibration, but the established/probable/possible/unresolved structure, named uncertainty sources, and identified resolution step meet the Score 5 anchor.
